turns.replyText:
Can you explain the main options in simple terms?

Love that you’re diving into this! Let’s keep it really simple and focus on the main choices you’ll see when you’re picking a rose.

Shape of the plant (how it grows)
Shrub/bush roses: Look like a rounded bush. Great for most gardens and beginners.
Climbing roses: Long canes that need a support (arch, fence, trellis). Good if you want a rose-covered arch or wall.
Groundcover/landscape roses: Low and wide. Good for covering a slope or the front of a bed.
Hybrid tea roses: Classic “long-stem” roses, usually one big flower per stem, great for cutting for vases.
Size Every rose page shows height and width in feet.
Smaller (2–3 ft): good for pots or small spaces.
Medium (3–5 ft): good for most garden beds.
Large (5+ ft): more of a statement plant or climber.
Sun & climate
Full sun = at least 6 hours of direct sunlight daily. Most roses like this.
Partial shade = 4+ hours of sun; some roses will still do well.
Hardiness zone: This is your climate rating. Use the zone selector at the top of our website so you only see roses that will live in your area.
Bloom style & how often they bloom
Repeat or continuous bloomers: Flower, rest, flower again all season. Easiest for beginners.
Once-blooming: One big flush of flowers, then mostly foliage the rest of the year.
Flower type: Single (few petals, simple), semi-double, or very full/rosette (lots of petals, “English rose” look).
Fragrance
You’ll see notes like light, moderate, or strong fragrance.
If scent matters a lot to you, choose moderate or strong.
Color Just pick what makes you happiest: pinks, reds, apricots, whites, etc. The filters on the “Shop All Roses” page let you sort by color.

turns.replyText:
How do I use it properly the very first time?

Great question to ask before you even hit “checkout.” Let’s keep this really simple.

I want to be sure I’m guiding you on the right thing: are you asking how to use

your new rose the first time (how to plant it),
the Get Growing Bundle, or
the Founders Fish Fertilizer the first time?

I’ll outline the basic “first use” steps for a new rose plus amendments, and you can tell me which part you want more detail on.

When your rose arrives (first-time setup)
Unpack it and water the pot well.
Keep it outdoors in a bright spot for a day or two if you can plant soon.
Plan to get it into the ground or a larger container within about 2 weeks, timed for after your last spring frost or at least 6 weeks before your first fall frost.
Planting the rose the first time
Choose a sunny spot (6+ hours of direct sun) with soil that drains well.
Dig roughly a 2 ft wide, 2 ft deep hole.
Mix some organic matter (like compost) into the soil you removed.
Set the rose so the base of the stems is at the same level it was in the pot.
Backfill with your improved soil, press gently to remove big air pockets.
Water deeply so everything settles.
Add a thin layer of compost or mulch on top to help keep moisture in (but not piled against the stems).
Using amendments/fertilizer the first time
Soil amendments (like compost) get mixed into the planting hole soil or used as a thin layer on top.
Gentle liquid fertilizer (like a fish fertilizer) is usually:
Diluted in water according to the label, then
Watered around the base of the plant, not on dry roots and not on hot, dry soil at midday.
